newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down, Nov FOMC minutes show bias.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down, Nov FOMC minutes show bias.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices ended lower on Friday after profit-taking dragged prices off early peaks and disappointment with a nuance of Federal Reserve policy prompted late selling in thin trade.

The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond ended at 98-20/32, down 8/32, its lowest level of the day. The 30-year bond yield ended at 6.61 percent, up from 6.586 percent at the close on Thursday -- when the market rallied.
The market spent most of the day trading in very narrow ranges, gathering no momentum in any direction.
"After the market rallied on Thursday, people had a better sense that the market had value," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets.

"That price action helped us to define our range for the time as being between 6-1/4 percent and 6-3/4 percent (on the 30-year bond yield) without any tendency to touch on the extremes of that range," he said.
The market opened higher, encouraged that the gains from Thursday's rally had been retained in overnight trade.
The government's revision of third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to 2.1 percent left the market unperturbed.

"There was nothing there," said Karydakis of the GDP figures. "There was a little fine tuning of various components -- consumption was a little lower than previous reported and inventories were a little higher -- but the profile of third- quarter GDP as one of moderate growth didn't change in any appreciable way."
"The numbers were a non-event," agreed Michelle Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities.
After about an hour of trading, some players decided to take profits, said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities Inc.
"A lot of people who had made money buying notes during the auction process took profits," said Dimick.
The Treasury sold $18.25 billion in two-year notes on Wednesday and $12.5 billion in a well-received five-year auction on Thursday.

"If you bought five-year notes at 6.165 percent in Thursday's auction at the peak on Friday morning those notes were yielding 6.08 percent; you made a quick 8.5 basis points in half a day on your new five-year notes," said Dimick.
As players tried to capture some of those gains, "we saw outright profit-taking from real money accounts," he said.
Analysts were heartened by the ability of the futures market to settle above Thursday's levels. The March T-bonds were up 5/32 to 113-10/32 at the end of pit trade in Chicago.

But the late-afternoon release of minutes from the November 13 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, the policy-making arm of the Federal Reserve, pushed the market -- which had been showing some very slight losses -- deeper into the minus column.
While the Fed voted 12-0 at its November meeting to keep interest rates steady, it also decided to retain a bias toward tightening in its policy directive.

Prices drifted to session lows in thin trade after the FOMC minutes were released. Traders had said the market could edge higher if the FOMC policy directive were shifted to neutral and there was some "marginal disappointment" when the bias toward tightening was retained, said Marilyn Schaja, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.

Short-term rates finished higher with three-month bill rates up four basis points to 4.90 percent and six-month and year-bill rates up two basis points each to 5.06 percent and 5.21 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes slipped 2/32 to 99-26/32, yielding 5.85 percent. Five-year notes slid 5/32 to 99-29/32, yielding 99-29/32.
Ten-year notes dropped 7/32 to 101 even, yielding 6.36 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk ((212-859-1679))
